title: What's actually worth automating in your work
promise: You'll walk away with four things. Your tasks ranked by the hours they cost you a year. One candidate chosen. The math done on how many months it takes to pay for itself. And a written list of what you'll never automate.
why: Javier does home renovations in Zaragoza. He spent three weekends, twenty-two hours, building a system to write his quotes for him. He does four quotes a month and each one took him twenty minutes: sixteen hours a year. In other words, it would take a year and four months to recoup the time invested. And five months in, the whole thing stopped working. Meanwhile, he was answering "what time are you coming tomorrow?" twelve times a day. Two minutes each time: a hundred and six hours a year. That could've been fixed with two saved messages on his phone and a calendar link. Two hours of work. He automated what annoyed him instead of what cost him. That's almost everyone's mistake.

theory.title: The math fits on a napkin
theory.text: Automating has a reward and it has a price, and almost nobody writes down both. The reward is calculated like this: minutes it takes, times how many times a month you do it, times twelve, divided by sixty. That gives you hours a year. It's the only unit you can use to compare tasks that have nothing to do with each other. The price is the hours it takes to build it, plus the hours it'll cost you to maintain every year. The practical rule: if the annual reward doesn't beat the price within twelve months, don't build it yet. And put a number on your hour even if it feels awkward, because decisions are much easier to make in dollars. If your hour is worth $30, saving forty-eight hours a year is $1,440. With that figure in front of you, you already know whether it's worth a Saturday. The math isn't exact and it doesn't need to be: it's not there to impress, it's there to rule things out.
theory.analogy: It's the same math you do with a kitchen appliance. A $90 bread maker you've used twice and that lives in the attic is extremely expensive. A $20 kettle you turn on four times a day is the best purchase in the house. It's not the price that decides, it's how many times you touch it.
theory.example: Elena runs an art supply store in Granada. She hates the quarterly VAT filing: four hours of agony, four times a year, sixteen hours annually. What she doesn't hate is answering "do you have it in stock?" on Instagram, because she doesn't even register it as work. That's four minutes, fifteen times a week: forty-eight hours a year. At $30 an hour, the filing costs her $480 a year and the Instagram messages $1,440. She spent a whole weekend fighting the $480 one and it never occurred to her to look at the $1,440 one.

theory.title: Frequency beats duration almost every time
theory.text: Your brain scores tasks by how much they annoy you, not by what they cost you. And what takes two minutes never annoys you, so it becomes invisible. That's why a four-hour task you do four times a year feels like a monster: sixteen hours. And a four-minute one you do fifteen times a week feels like nothing: forty-eight hours. The practical consequence: any list you write from memory will be wrong, always, and in the same direction. You'll get the minutes right and the frequency wrong. That's why the first task in this lesson is measuring five real days, not thinking harder. Now, the honest nuance: the math isn't the only criterion. There are three kinds of task worth automating even when the numbers don't add up. Ones you don't do out of avoidance, and not doing them costs you money, like chasing unpaid invoices. Ones you do carelessly and get wrong, and the mistake is costly, like checking that every invoice has the correct tax ID. And ones you literally can't do at all right now, like transcribing two hundred customer calls to see what they're asking for. Those three get a pass on the arithmetic.
theory.analogy: A dripping faucet worries nobody, because each drop is negligible. A twenty-minute shower does worry people, because it's noticeable. By the end of the month the faucet has used more water than the shower, and it still worries nobody.
theory.example: Javier, the renovation guy, had both sitting in front of him. The quotes: twenty minutes, four times a month, sixteen hours a year, and they weighed on him like a stone because they require thinking. The "what time are you coming?" messages: two minutes, twelve times a day, a hundred and six hours a year. They weighed nothing, because you answer them with your thumb while walking. He automated the sixteen hours and not the hundred and six. His brain gave him the list backward, and there was no way to know it without writing it down.

theory.title: The real price: building it, maintaining it, and reviewing it
theory.text: When people calculate what it costs to automate something, they only count the time spent building it. And it's three bills, not one. The first is the build, and your estimate is going to be optimistic. Multiply what you think it'll take by three. And multiply the AI's estimate by three again, since it's even more optimistic than you are. The second is maintenance, because automations rot on their own. The website you were pulling data from gets redesigned, the app changes a menu, the model gets updated and answers differently, a price goes up. Budget between two and six hours a year for every living automation. Go with the high number if it depends on a page or app you don't control. The third bill is the one almost nobody sees: the time spent reviewing the output. If you automate something that used to take ten minutes to do, and checking the result takes you seven, you haven't saved ten minutes, you've saved three. And here's the real danger, and it isn't that it breaks. It's the silent failure: the thing stops working without throwing a single error. And it spends three weeks returning empty or wrong results that nobody's looked at.
theory.analogy: A dog doesn't cost what you paid for it. It costs the food, the vet, the grooming, and fifteen years of seven-a.m. walks in the rain. Nobody decides to adopt by looking only at the adoption fee, and yet that's exactly how people decide to automate.
theory.example: Nuria is a dietitian in Bilbao and puts together about thirty meal plans a month. By hand it takes her twenty-five minutes each. With AI the draft comes out in one. But checking allergies, quantities, and that the same dish hasn't repeated three days running takes her eighteen. The real saving is six minutes per plan, not twenty-four: three hours a month instead of twelve. It's still worth it to her, but it's a quarter of what she'd calculated. And that difference is exactly what decides whether she gives it a Saturday or two.

theory.title: Automating and assisting aren't the same, and you almost always want assisting
theory.text: Automating means the thing happens on its own: it fires, does its job, and finishes, whether you're watching or asleep. Assisting means the machine leaves you the work half done and you look at it, fix it, and send it. It sounds like the same thing and it's nothing alike. The assisted version gets built in an afternoon instead of three weekends. It can't break dangerously, because there are always eyes on it before it goes out. And it has practically no maintenance. With that in hand, your tasks fall into four boxes. One: it repeats, the steps are always the same, and your judgment isn't needed. Plus, if it goes wrong you notice in under a minute. That gets automated. Two: it repeats but your judgment is involved. That gets assisted. Three: it happens fewer than twice a month. That gets done by hand, no matter how boring it is. Four: there's money, other people's data, a client waiting, or something that can't be undone. That doesn't get touched. The doubt will always be between one and two, and there's a rule that never fails: if you're unsure, it's two.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between a dishwasher and a kitchen helper. You load the dishwasher and walk away: it always does the same thing and if it goes wrong you see it when you open it. The helper leaves you the onion chopped and the stock ready, but you're the one who plates the dish. Because the seasoning is what people are paying to eat.
theory.example: A wedding photographer in Seville has two tasks that look like the same one. Renaming twelve hundred photos from "IMG_4471.JPG" to "2026-05-30-wedding-lucia-hugo-0001.jpg" gets automated. The rule is fixed, no judgment involved, and a mistake shows up at a glance. Choosing the sixty photos that go in the album doesn't get automated, because that's exactly what he's paid for. What the AI can do is filter out the three hundred blurry or eyes-closed shots and leave him nine hundred to look through. That's assisting: it takes off the dumb work and hands him back his own.

theory.title: The blacklist: what never gets automated
theory.text: There's one rule that, on its own, prevents almost every disaster: the machine prepares, the person presses. Anything that can't be undone stays in draft, waiting for someone to press the button. Sending a client an email, making a payment, deleting files, publishing something, canceling an order, answering a complaint. All of that gets prepared on its own and sent by hand. Second group: anything whose mistake isn't visible at a glance. Figures that end up on an invoice, medical data, contract terms, prices. Anything that, if it comes out wrong, looks just as well-written as if it comes out right. Third: anything with other people's personal data traveling to places you haven't checked. Fourth, and this one stings: don't automate the judgment you're paid for. If you're a consultant and you automate the advice, you haven't saved time. You've given away your craft, and on top of that you stop seeing the patterns that made you good at it. And a last one that seems obvious and everyone skips: don't automate something you don't know how to do by hand. If you don't know how to do it, you can't judge whether the output is correct. And an automation whose output you can't evaluate isn't a help: it's a source of errors with good presentation.
theory.analogy: In a print shop nobody lets the machine run five thousand copies without someone having signed off on the color proof first. It's not distrust of the machine: it's that five thousand badly printed copies don't get picked back up off the floor.
theory.example: An accounting firm in Alicante connected a system that issued and sent the month's invoices automatically. On day one the trigger fired twice because of a tool glitch. Sixty clients got a duplicate invoice and the books ended up with sixty ghost entries. Two full days undoing it and an awkward call with every big client. The same system leaving the invoices in draft, with a person pressing "send" after looking at the list, would have cost three minutes a month. And nothing would have happened that day at all.

theory.title: Start at the cheapest step, not at the system
theory.text: "Automate customer support" isn't a project, it's a wish. A project is: take the voice note a client sends and turn it into a card with name, address, and what they want. One input, one output, one piece. Projects die trying to solve the whole process at once. And on top of that there's a four-step ladder almost nobody climbs in order. First, a saved piece of text you paste into the AI's box each time. Second, a project with fixed instructions and your files inside. Third, a small program you run yourself when you want. And fourth, real automation, with a trigger that fires it on its own. Each step costs roughly five times more than the one before, and you only climb it once the one below starts genuinely bothering you. There are two more conditions before touching anything. One: you've done that task at least five times by hand in the last few weeks. Otherwise you don't yet know what it's really like, and you'll end up automating an imaginary version of it. Two: you've written down a list of five things to check in thirty seconds to know whether the result is wrong. If you can't write that list, you're not ready to automate it.
theory.analogy: Nobody buys a van to move house once: you borrow your brother-in-law's. If you end up borrowing it every two weeks and you're already embarrassed to ask, then yes, buy the van. But in that order.
theory.example: Carlos handles communications for a running club in Oviedo and wanted to "automate social media." He started with one piece: turning Sunday's race results into an Instagram post. First step, a saved piece of text in his phone's notes that he pastes into Claude along with the results. Twenty minutes to write it well, and it saves him twenty-five minutes every Sunday. Forty races a year is sixteen hours saved in exchange for twenty minutes of work. He's been there for eight months and still hasn't needed to climb a step, and that's a win, not laziness.

tasks.title: Write down for five days what you actually do
tasks.where: In a note on your phone or a notebook open next to your keyboard. No spreadsheets.
tasks.action: For five straight working days, every time you finish something you'd already done before, write it down in one line. Write what it was and how many minutes, rounded to five. For example: "Answering a client on WhatsApp about the schedule — 5." "Entering an invoice into Excel — 10." "Looking up a material's price on the supplier's site — 5." Don't do it from memory at the end of the day. Memory is exactly where the two-minute things vanish, and those are the ones that weigh most. Also write down what you do from your phone away from the computer, which is usually half of it. If you forget one day, don't start over: keep going and count four days instead of five.
tasks.expect: Between thirty and eighty lines after five days, with many repeated and with different minutes between them. If you have fewer than twenty lines, you're not writing down the small stuff, and the small stuff is where the money is.
tasks.stuck: If you keep forgetting, set a phone alarm every two hours that says "what did I just do?" When it goes off, write down everything from that stretch at once. And if the idea of measuring five days is blocking you, measure just one: one measured day is worth infinitely more than five imagined ones.

tasks.title: Have the AI turn that list into hours per year
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in a new, empty conversation
tasks.action: Open a new conversation (don't reuse one that already has things in it, since it drags context along and pollutes the answer). Copy the prompt below. Where it says "PASTE YOUR LIST HERE," paste in the lines from the previous task exactly as they are, with their typos, their disorder, and their abbreviations. Don't clean them up first: that job is precisely what you're handing over to it. Send it and wait for the table.
tasks.prompt:
You're my process analyst. I'm handing you the log of what I've done over five working days, written by hand, messy and abbreviated.

[PASTE YOUR LIST HERE]

Do this, in this order:

1. Group whatever is the same task even if I wrote it with different words. If I wrote "answer Marta about the deadline" and "reply about when we're delivering," that's one task.
2. For each grouped task, tell me how many times it shows up across the five days and how many minutes they add up to.
3. Extrapolate to a 22-working-day month and an 11-month working year.
4. Give me a table sorted highest to lowest by HOURS PER YEAR, with these exact columns: Task | Times a month | Minutes each time | Hours a year | Are the steps always the same? (yes / mostly / no) | Can I tell in 30 seconds if the result is wrong? (yes / no)
5. Below the table write two short paragraphs. In the first, the three tasks eating the most hours. In the second, tasks eating few hours but that I described with annoyed-sounding words, so I can see with my own eyes the difference between what bothers me and what costs me.

Don't invent tasks that aren't in my list. If you don't understand something, put it in a separate section called "I didn't understand this" instead of guessing. If the minutes add up to more than a working day fits, warn me that I logged something wrong.
tasks.expect: A table of eight to fifteen rows, sorted by hours a year. And almost certainly a surprise in the top three. Something you did without noticing that turns out to eat over fifty hours a year.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you a table with suspiciously round numbers or tasks you never wrote, it made them up. Tell it: "You added tasks that aren't in my list. Redo the table using only my lines, and if you don't understand a line, copy it verbatim into the not-understood section." If the table looks bad on mobile, ask: "Give me the same thing as a list, one task per block, no table."

tasks.title: Sort each task into the four boxes
tasks.where: In the same AI conversation, right below the table
tasks.action: Without opening a new conversation, paste the prompt below right after the table it just gave you. You're giving it fixed rules to classify by, instead of letting it improvise. Pay special attention to the final section, which is the one that's actually useful. That's where it'll tell you what you wanted to automate out of enthusiasm and shouldn't.
tasks.prompt:
Now sort those same tasks into four boxes. These are the rules, and don't change or soften them:

- AUTOMATE: the task repeats, the steps are always the same, my judgment isn't needed, and if the result comes out wrong I notice in under a minute.
- ASSIST: it repeats, but my judgment is involved. The machine prepares a draft and I review it and send it. Nothing ever goes out without me having seen it.
- DO BY HAND: it happens fewer than twice a month, no matter how boring.
- DON'T TOUCH: there's money involved, other people's data, a client waiting on the other end, something that can't be undone, or it's exactly the professional judgment I'm paid for.

For each task tell me which box and one single sentence explaining why that one and not the next one over. If you're torn between AUTOMATE and ASSIST, always pick ASSIST and say you were torn.

At the end write a section titled "You're getting ahead of yourself" where you flag the tasks I probably want to automate out of excitement and that, by these rules, shouldn't be. Be blunt in that section, don't agree with me out of politeness.
tasks.expect: Every task with its box and its reason, and almost certainly more tasks in ASSIST than in AUTOMATE. That's not a mistake: it's the correct split for someone starting out.
tasks.stuck: If it puts almost everything in AUTOMATE, it's being agreeable. Reply: "You're being optimistic. Go through the list again and for every task you put in AUTOMATE, tell me exactly what would happen the day the result comes out wrong and nobody looks at it. If the answer is uncomfortable, move it to ASSIST."

tasks.title: Write your blacklist and ask it to attack it
tasks.where: First on paper or in a note, then in the AI app
tasks.action: Before opening anything, write by hand five things in your work you wouldn't let happen on their own even if they worked perfectly. Think about things that can't be undone and things where the mistake isn't visible. Then open a new conversation and paste the prompt below with your list inside. Save the final answer wherever you keep your work stuff. This list is what's going to stop you six months from now, once you're feeling brave.
tasks.prompt:
This is what I do for a living: [DESCRIBE YOUR WORK IN TWO SENTENCES: what you do, who your client is, and the worst thing that can happen if you make a mistake].

This is my list of things I've decided to never automate:
[PASTE YOUR LIST]

Do three things:

1. For each item on my list, tell me which of these four is the real reason: "can't be undone," "the mistake isn't visible," "there's a person waiting on the other end," or "it's my professional judgment." If an item doesn't fit any of the four, tell me clearly, because maybe that one actually could be automated and I put it there out of fear.
2. Add what's missing from my list given my specific line of work. Think about legal obligations, personal data, money, and reputation. Be specific to my industry: don't give me advice that would apply to anyone.
3. For each item on the final list, tell me what the ASSISTED version that would actually be safe looks like: exactly what the machine prepares and exactly what I do before it goes out.

Don't tell me "be careful." Tell me exactly what specific step stays in my hands.
tasks.expect: A final list of eight to twelve items, each with its reason and its assisted version next to it. The useful part is the assisted versions: they show you that almost nothing is fully off-limits, only off-limits without someone in front of it.
tasks.stuck: If you get generic advice like "be careful with sensitive data," you didn't tell it clearly enough what you do. Go back to the start of the prompt and write four very specific sentences. Say what you sell, to whom, what document you handle most, and what would happen to you if that document reached the wrong person.

tasks.title: Calculate your top candidate's break-even point
tasks.where: In the AI app, new conversation
tasks.action: Take the task that ended up first in the AUTOMATE or ASSIST box (not the one you feel like doing most: the first on the list). Paste the prompt below describing it in detail. When it gives you the build hours, multiply them by three yourself before deciding anything. The AI is systematically optimistic about time, and with you it'll be doubly so. If, with the number tripled, the break-even point goes beyond twelve months, cross that task out. Try the next one on the list.
tasks.prompt:
I want to automate this: [DESCRIBE THE TASK IN FIVE SENTENCES: what comes in, what you do with it, what comes out, where each thing lives (email, WhatsApp, a folder, a spreadsheet, a website), and how many times a month you do it].

About me: I've never coded. I work by typing in the AI's text box, not in a terminal. I use Windows.

Answer me with exactly this:

1. The three simplest ways to solve it, ordered from least to most work: the "saved text I paste each time" version, the "project with fixed instructions and my files inside" version, and the "runs on its own with a trigger" version. For each: what it does and what it does NOT do.
2. For each version, how many hours of my time it costs to build, given that I'm someone who's never coded. Give me the high, pessimistic number, not the pretty one.
3. What parts of each version are going to break on their own over time and how often I'd have to touch them.
4. How much it costs a month in dollars, if it costs anything, and whether I need to put a card in anywhere.
5. Each version's break-even point: how many months until I recover the time I invested building it.
6. A final sentence in this exact format: "I'd start with ___ and wouldn't move to the next one until ___."

If you think this task isn't worth automating, tell me in the first line of your answer and explain why before answering anything else.
tasks.expect: Three versions with hours, dollars, and payoff months, plus a final sentence telling you where to start. In the vast majority of cases that sentence will point to the first step, the saved text, and that's good news.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you you'll build it in twenty minutes, don't believe it and reply: "That number is for someone who's already done this before. Give me the estimate for someone who's going to get it wrong three times, won't understand half the screens, and has never coded." If it suggests installing things or opening the terminal at the first step, reply: "Give me a version that works just by typing in the AI's text box, with nothing installed."

tasks.title: Build the cheapest step: the saved text
tasks.where: In the AI app, and then in your phone's notes or a document
tasks.action: Before building the reusable prompt (the saved text you'll paste each time) you need three real examples. They have to be actual cases of that task done by hand: what came in and what came out. Look for them in your email, your WhatsApp, or your folders, and copy them. Then paste the prompt below with those three examples inside. Save whatever it gives you somewhere you can reach in two taps from your phone. A note pinned at the top works, or a document with a name in capital letters. Saved text you can't find is text that doesn't exist.
tasks.prompt:
Let's write the script I'm going to reuse every time I do this task. The task is: [DESCRIBE IT IN TWO SENTENCES].

Here are three real examples of how I've done it by hand, with what came in and what came out:

EXAMPLE 1 — Came in: [...] / Came out: [...]
EXAMPLE 2 — Came in: [...] / Came out: [...]
EXAMPLE 3 — Came in: [...] / Came out: [...]

Write me a text I can paste as-is every time, with gaps marked as [LIKE THIS] only for the parts that change from one time to the next. It should include:
- What role you should take on.
- What information I'll give you and in what order.
- The exact format I want for the answer, with sections named one by one.
- What you should NOT do, and what you should write if you're missing a piece of data, instead of making it up.

Then, and this is the most important part, write me a FIVE-POINT CHECKLIST I can look at in thirty seconds to know whether the answer is good or bad. All five points have to be things you check with your eyes, not opinions. "All three sections show up" counts. "The tone is appropriate" doesn't.
tasks.expect: A text of fifteen to forty lines with marked gaps, plus a list of five concrete checks at the end. That five-point list is what you're really going to take away from this lesson.
tasks.stuck: If the checklist comes out full of vague stuff ("that it's clear," "that it sounds professional"), send it back: "These points are opinions, not checks. Rewrite them so each one can be answered yes or no by looking at the text for three seconds, with no thinking." If you don't have three real examples because you've never done the task, don't automate it yet: do it five times by hand first.

tasks.title: Use it five times by hand and time it
tasks.where: In your real work, over a week or two
tasks.action: Use the saved text on five real cases, not made-up tests. Each time write down two numbers in the same note. One: the total minutes it took (pasting, waiting, reviewing, and fixing). Two: how many of your five checklist points failed. Compare that total to what it used to take you before, which you already measured in the first task. This step is the one almost everyone skips, and it's the only one that tells you the truth. Up to now everything was estimates, and from here on it's data.
tasks.expect: Five pairs of numbers. It's normal for the first case to go worse than by hand, and for time to drop clearly from the third case onward. If by the fifth case you're still taking as long as by hand, the task wasn't a good candidate, or the saved text needs another pass.
tasks.stuck: If the same checklist points keep failing, don't rewrite the whole text. Go back to the conversation and write "These two points always fail: [which ones]. Add a specific instruction to the script so it stops happening, and leave the rest of the script exactly the same." If something different fails each time, the task involves more judgment than you thought and permanently belongs in the ASSIST box.

tasks.title: Decide who presses the button and how you'll find out if it fails
tasks.where: In a document or a note, next to the saved text
tasks.action: Write half a page with six lines, and save it right next to the automation. One: exactly what it does and what it doesn't. Two: what comes in and where that data comes from. Three: who reviews it before it goes out (if the answer is "nobody," that's only okay if nothing like it appears on your blacklist). Four: how you're going to find out it's stopped working. Here the only thing that works is something you check at a fixed moment, because a silent failure isn't going to warn you. Five: what you do if it fails, written as steps, including how to go back to doing it by hand. Six: a date within ninety days to check whether it's still working and still saving what it said it would. Put that date on your phone's calendar right now, not when you're done.
tasks.expect: Half a page with the six lines answered plainly, and a ninety-day reminder on the calendar. If line four was hard to write, that's a sign the automation could break without anyone noticing. And that's exactly what needs fixing before you let it loose.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know how you'd find out about a failure, use the dumbest thing that works. Have the task itself leave its result somewhere you pass by every day. A note, a folder, or a message to yourself all work. And check if there's anything new today. If there's nothing new when there should be, you've already found out. That's worth more than any fancy monitoring system you're not going to build.

matters: Counting the number of times, not the annoyance. Almost everyone automates what irritates them and leaves what eats their life untouched. What gets dealt with in two minutes never hurts, and it still adds up to a hundred hours a year. Skip the five-day measurement and you'll spend your Saturdays on exactly what matters least. And feel very productive doing it.

Writing down maintenance and review time before deciding, not after. Building is the small part: the expensive part is it breaking on its own five months from now, and the time it takes to check every result. An automation whose output has to be fully reviewed doesn't save anything, it just swaps writing for reading, and reading with distrust is more tiring than writing.

Writing the blacklist before the scare, not after. Anything that can't be undone (sending, paying, deleting, publishing, canceling) gets prepared on its own but pressed by a person. That single rule prevents the vast majority of disasters and costs three minutes a month. Skipping it costs two days undoing sixty duplicate invoices and an awkward call with every client.

Starting at the cheapest step even if it feels small. A saved text you paste into the AI's box gets built in half an hour. It never breaks, costs nothing, and tells you whether the idea was good. Skip that step and build the full system directly, and you'll pay for it. You'll discover twenty hours in that the task wasn't what you thought it was.
ignore: The named tools: Zapier, Make, n8n, and the twenty others out there. Their starter plans run from $0 to about $25 a month and they all do roughly the same thing. Choosing between them is a decision for three months from now, and right now it changes nothing, because you don't yet know what you're going to automate.

Automating the whole process end to end. "Handle customers" isn't a project. A piece with a clear input and a clear output is. Once you've got three pieces working, you'll see for yourself where they connect, without anyone explaining it.

Measuring to the second with a stopwatch and a spreadsheet. Rounding to five minutes already tells apart perfectly what eats a hundred hours a year from what eats ten. That's the only distinction you need. Extra precision doesn't change a single decision, and it does make you quit measuring by day two.
canDo: Do the arithmetic and sort your list, if you give it the data. It can group tasks you wrote with different words, add up minutes, turn totals into hours per year, and rank them highest to lowest. You supply the observation, it supplies the math and the order.

Find the repeated step hidden inside a long, disorganized description of your day. Tell it how you work in three badly written paragraphs and it'll point out the three things you always do the same way. Including ones you no longer notice from habit.

Do the actual dumb work, which is where almost all the savings live. For example: pulling data out of a text, converting something into a fixed format, sorting messages into categories, summarizing, transcribing, renaming according to a rule.

Write you the reusable text and, above all, the five-point checklist to review it. Ask it: "give me five things I can check with my eyes in thirty seconds to know if this is wrong." It's probably the single most valuable thing you'll do with it in the whole course.
cantDo: Know how many times a month you do something. It doesn't see you work. Give it a made-up frequency and it'll hand you back a beautiful table built on a fake number. And that table will look exactly as convincing as a real one.

Honestly estimate how long it'll take you to build it. It's always optimistic, and always in the same direction: it'll tell you "you'll have this in twenty minutes" and it'll be three hours. Multiply what it tells you by three and you'll be much closer than it is.

Find out its own work has been coming out wrong for three weeks. It doesn't review what it did yesterday and doesn't compare. It has no way of knowing the website it was pulling prices from got redesigned in March. The silent failure gets caught by you, or by nobody.

Decide what mistake you can afford in your business. What an angry client is worth. What your insurance covers. What's at stake if someone's personal data ends up where it shouldn't. It knows none of that, and above all, it isn't going to own it for you when it happens.
words: Automate
Letting something happen on its own, without you present. It kicks off, does its job, and finishes, whether you're asleep or on vacation.
Assist
The machine leaves the work half done and you look at it, fix it, and send it. Nothing leaves your hands without you having seen it with your own eyes.
Break-even point
The moment what you've saved equals what it cost you to build. From that day on, everything it saves is pure gain.
Human in the loop
Having a person in the middle of the process who has to give the go-ahead for it to continue. It's the handbrake on any automation.
Silent failure
When something stops working and doesn't warn you. No red alert shows up: it's simply been returning empty or wrong results for three weeks and nobody's noticed.
Maintenance
The time you have to spend every year fixing something that used to work. Everything around it changed: the page it pulled data from, the price, the menu of the app it used.
Trigger
The signal that kicks off the process: an email arriving, it being eight in the morning, someone filling out a form.
Saved prompt

A text you write well once, with gaps for the little that changes. You copy and paste it every time you do the same task. It's the cheapest way there is to repeat something without repeating the effort.
Workflow
The whole chain of steps from something coming in to a result coming out.
Irreversible
Something that can't be undone. A sent email, a payment made, a file deleted for good, a post people have already seen.
